title: Inquest into death of Jordan Norfield in Prince Albert rescheduled for next week
subtitle: Jordan Norfield was "a loving, fun, resilient, and bright young man who made friends wherever he went," his family said.
article: An inquest into the 2020 death of a 30-year-old man after his transfer from Prince Albert police custody to Victoria Hospital has been rescheduled for next week.

The inquest into the death of Jordan Norfield, previously scheduled at the Coronet Hotel in Prince Albert earlier this year, will now be held from Oct. 30 to Nov. 3. Lawyer Tim Hawryluk will preside as coroner.
The Saskatchewan government said a June media release that the inquest had been adjourned at the request of his family's counsel.
Norfield died at Victoria Hospital on Dec. 5, 2020 after he was transferred there from police custody by ambulance, the province has said.

A lawyer representing Norfield's mother, Sandy Pitzel, provided a statement to media on the family's behalf on Thursday and said the family looks forward to the inquest and any recommendations the jury makes in the hope that more tragic deaths like his can be prevented.

"She and her side of her family have many questions about how their beloved son, brother, and nephew went from being physically healthy on November 30th, 2020 to dying five days later, on December 5th, 2020," the statement said.

Prince Albert police said in a media release in December 2020 that Norfield was initially taken into custody on Dec. 1, 2020 on a detention order under the provincial Public Health Act, was put into police detention cells overnight and was taken to Victoria Hospital the next morning for assessment and treatment. They said they were later told he died on Dec. 5, 2020.
Norfield's family remembers him as "a loving, fun, resilient, and bright young man who made friends wherever he went," their statement said.

He travelled all over the country for work and planned to go to school to study mechanics before his death. In the month before he died, he was accepted into a yearlong treatment program for alcohol use, it added.
"Although Jordan had some struggles, he was a story of resiliency, strength, and perseverance. He had been making great strides toward change and was working hard to improve his life."

Inquests are a public fact-finding, not fault-finding, process that establishes who died, when and how. The process may also highlight dangerous conditions or practices, and the six-member jury can make non-binding recommendations.
